title: Classical and jazz
subtitle: Works, records and the people behind them
about: Landmark works from Allegri to Górecki and the jazz records, tunes and nicknames worth knowing. Each card names the composer or leader, and the notes flag credits that are shared, disputed or misattributed.

cards.note: Published with four sonnets, possibly by the composer himself, each split into three parts to match the three movements of its concerto.
First performed in Dublin for charity; standing for the Hallelujah chorus rests on a story about George II with no convincing evidence.
Presented to the Margrave of Brandenburg in 1721; the tale that they then sat unplayed in his library is disputed by scholars.
About 50 musicians played it on a barge on the Thames; George I was so pleased he had it repeated at least three times.

cards.prompt: Toccata and Fugue in D minor
cards.note: Long credited to Bach, though a minority of scholars have questioned his authorship since 1981; Stokowski's orchestration featured in Disney's Fantasia.
Forgotten for centuries until Jean-François Paillard's slow, lush 1968 recording made it a hit; the oldest surviving manuscript dates from around 1840.
Named after harpsichordist Johann Gottlieb Goldberg; Forkel's story that they were written to soothe an insomniac count is now widely doubted.
A public rehearsal reportedly drew over 12,000 people, jamming London Bridge for three hours; at the actual display a pavilion caught fire.
Mendelssohn, aged 20, revived it in Berlin in 1829, the central event in the nineteenth-century rediscovery of Bach's music.
Written for the coronation of George II, it has been sung before the anointing at every British coronation since.
According to a letter by Leopold Mozart, his 14-year-old son heard it in the Sistine Chapel and wrote it out from memory.
Usually credited to Albinoni, it was composed by his biographer Giazotto, supposedly from a bass-line fragment whose existence is still debated.
Mozart's own catalogue lists five movements, but one minuet is lost; the serenade was not published until about 1827.
Dedicated to Countess Giulietta Guicciardi; the nickname grew later from moonlit imagery the poet Ludwig Rellstab attached to it.
Published only in 1867, forty years after the composer's death; 'Elise' may be a misreading, and Therese Malfatti is the most popular candidate.
At the premiere the deaf composer was still beating time when contralto Caroline Unger turned him round to see the applause.
Unfinished at Mozart's death; Süssmayr completed it for Count Walsegg, who commissioned it in memory of his wife and probably meant to claim it.
According to Ferdinand Ries, the composer tore the title page in half on hearing that Napoleon had declared himself emperor.
Asked if the sudden loud chord was meant to wake the audience, Haydn said no: he simply wanted to surprise London with something new.
His last and longest symphony; the nickname was probably coined by the London impresario Johann Peter Salomon.
Inspired by hearing Handel oratorios in London; at 'Let there be light', an eyewitness said the orchestra could not continue for several minutes.
Its slow movement varies the composer's own hymn for Emperor Francis II, a tune now sung as Germany's national anthem.
In the finale the players snuff their candles and leave one by one, a hint to Prince Esterházy that his musicians wanted to go home.
The finale of the Piano Sonata in A, K. 331, imitating the sound of Turkish Janissary bands; the composer himself titled it Alla turca.
Famous for its celesta, an instrument the composer had already used in The Voyevoda; the 1892 premiere was not considered a success.
The composer called separate concert performances 'an utter indiscretion' and forbade them until the complete Ring cycle opened at Bayreuth in 1876.
The composer told his patron it would be very loud and noisy but without artistic merit, because he wrote it without love.
Asked to sign a fan, Brahms wrote out its opening bars and added 'Unfortunately not by Johannes Brahms'.
Premiered at Carnegie Hall to thunderous applause; Neil Armstrong took a tape recording of it on the Apollo 11 mission in 1969.

cards.prompt: In the Hall of the Mountain King
cards.note: Written for Ibsen's Peer Gynt; the composer said it reeked so much of cowpats and ultra-Norwegianism that he could not bear to hear it.
Inspired by his obsession with the actress Harriet Smithson, who refused even to meet him; they married in 1833.
His friend Anselm Hüttenbrenner kept the manuscript for decades; the two completed movements were not premiered until 1865.
'Minute' means small, not sixty seconds; the French nickname, Waltz of the Little Dog, reportedly came from a dog chasing its tail.
Inspired by Nietzsche; the fanfare in Kubrick's 2001: A Space Odyssey was Karajan's 1959 recording with the Vienna Philharmonic.

cards.prompt: Piano Concerto No. 2 in C minor
cards.note: Dedicated to Nikolai Dahl, whose months of daily hypnotherapy helped the composer recover after his First Symphony's disastrous 1897 premiere.
Dedicated to Count László Teleki and published in 1851, it later became a favourite soundtrack for animated cartoons.
A memorial to his friend Viktor Hartmann's paintings; Ravel made the famous orchestration in 1922 on a commission from Koussevitzky.
Fearing it would harm his serious reputation, he banned public performance in his lifetime, releasing only The Swan for publication.
Dedicated 'to my friends pictured within'; each variation sketches someone in his circle, including his publisher August Jaeger as Nimrod.
Written in late 1874 after the composer had gone deaf, it follows the river Vltava from its two small source springs.
A covert protest against Russian censorship, it was performed under disguised names such as Happy Feelings at the Awakening of Finnish Spring.
Written at seventeen; sixteen years later he added incidental music for the play, including the famous Wedding March.
He chose texts from Luther's German Bible rather than the Latin Mass, aiming to comfort the living; his mother's death may have prompted it.
He found his finale at Hans von Bülow's funeral, where hearing a setting of Klopstock's resurrection hymn 'struck me like lightning'.
The 1913 Paris premiere provoked uproar in the theatre, later remembered as a riot; Nijinsky's choreography shocked as much as the music.
Commissioned by the dancer Ida Rubinstein; the composer called it seventeen minutes of 'orchestral tissue without music', one long crescendo.
Each movement reflects a planet's astrological character; Colin Matthews added Pluto, the Renewer in 2000, six years before Pluto's demotion.
Premiered with Paul Whiteman's band; clarinettist Ross Gorman played the opening run as a joke glissando, and the composer kept it.
Named after a Paul Verlaine poem, it is the third movement of the Suite bergamasque, begun around 1890 and revised before publication.
Toscanini premiered it on NBC radio in 1938; it was later played at Albert Einstein's funeral and broadcast after President Kennedy's.
Sets 24 poems from a medieval collection; 'O Fortuna', the chorus to the goddess of fortune, both opens and closes the work.
Commissioned by Natalya Sats of Moscow's Central Children's Theatre to introduce children to the instruments, each playing a character.
Inspired by George Meredith's 1881 poem; completed for violin and piano in 1914, it waited until 1920 for its first performance.
Written for choreographer Martha Graham, it includes variations on the Shaker tune Simple Gifts and won the Pulitzer Prize for Music.
After an anechoic chamber at Harvard still let him hear two sounds, his own body, he concluded that true silence cannot exist.
Played in besieged Leningrad in August 1942 by Karl Eliasberg's starving orchestra and broadcast by loudspeaker towards the German lines.
Commissioned by the actress Albertine Zehme, who premiered its 21 poems in Sprechstimme, a half-spoken, half-sung style.

cards.prompt: Quartet for the End of Time
cards.note: Written in a German prisoner-of-war camp and premiered there to about 400 prisoners and guards; the composer later claimed 5,000.
Written just before the composer left Soviet Estonia, in his tintinnabuli style; the title means 'mirror in the mirror'.
A 1992 release with soprano Dawn Upshaw sold over a million copies, probably the best-selling contemporary classical record.
Premiered two months before the composer's death; the librettist Emanuel Schikaneder played Papageno himself in his own Vienna theatre.
After the Venice premiere the composer wrote: 'La traviata last night a failure. Was the fault mine or the singers'?'
Its Paris premiere met a cool reception, and the composer died of heart disease three months later, aged 36.
Toscanini conducted the Turin premiere; Leoncavallo's rival opera on the same source, Murger's Paris vignettes, is now rarely staged.
Lorenzo Da Ponte adapted Beaumarchais's comedy, whose frank treatment of class conflict had led to its ban in Vienna as a play.
Reportedly composed in under three weeks; the Rome premiere was a disaster, with supporters of rival Paisiello jeering throughout.
Left unfinished at the composer's death; at the premiere Toscanini stopped mid-act and told the audience the maestro had died at this point.
Its opening Tristan chord is a landmark of chromatic harmony; Vienna abandoned a production after more than 70 rehearsals, sealing its unperformable reputation.
Written for the Mantua carnival, it is the earliest opera still regularly performed, though Peri's Dafne and Euridice came first.
Performed by 1689 at Josias Priest's girls' school in Chelsea; its climax is Dido's Lament, 'When I am laid in earth'.
His wife reportedly submitted the score on the final day of a publisher's competition; it was chosen as a finalist from 73 entries.
Based on George Crabbe's poem The Borough; Koussevitzky, who commissioned it, called it the greatest opera since Carmen.
Created with director Robert Wilson, it runs about five hours without an interval, and the audience may come and go freely.
